title: GTA in a neural network: an open world model, and the Summaryformer

GTA in a neural network: an open world model, and the Summaryformer

Community Article Published
November 15, 2026 Upvote 4 Abhishek Sensharma abhisheksensharma lucidml
Abhishek Sensharma, lucidml. November 2026.
Play it in your browser · Hugging Face Space · Weights and code · Architecture note

This is not the game. Every frame above is generated by a neural network while I hold the keys.

TL;DR

I trained a world model of GTA V. You give it one start image and hold WASD, and it generates the game one frame at a time while you play. There is no game engine underneath, the whole thing is a neural network.
It is a 630M-parameter transformer that I designed and trained from scratch. The weights and the complete inference code are open under Apache-2.0, and you can play it in the browser right now.

What it looks like

A minute of play, recorded from the browser demo. The clip starts with me picking a GTA V screenshot from Google Images as the start image.

Six frames from that session. All of them are generated.

The demo page. Before you press Play the window shows the starting frame, which is a real GTA V screenshot. After that, every frame comes from the model.
The rest of this post is about one part of the model: how it manages its context. I call the architecture Summaryformer.

Why memory is the problem

The model is causal, like an LLM. Every new frame attends to the frames before it through a KV cache, and that is the only way it knows where it is.
At 384x672 one frame is 1,008 tokens. If I keep the whole history window at full resolution, every token of a new frame attends to 26,208 keys, in all 28 blocks, on every denoising pass. That is too much work to stay playable. If I keep only a few frames instead, the model has almost no past to work with.
My bet is that the two kinds of past are not needed equally. A frame generated a moment ago matters in detail, because the next frame has to continue its motion pixel for pixel. A frame generated many seconds ago should matter only in outline: what was there, roughly where.
So in Summaryformer every frame is stored twice, at two sizes, and the model writes both itself.

A frame writes its own summary

Each frame goes into the transformer as one record:
record(t) = [ raw(t) : 1,008 tokens ] ++ [ sum(t) : 96 tokens ]

raw(t) is the frame's latent grid, one token per cell (24x42).
sum(t) is 96 summary tokens. They start from a learned init that is the same for every frame, they have no position on the grid, and they go through the same 28 blocks in the same forward pass as the raw tokens.

The summary tokens are all that later frames will get from this one, so training pushes them to hold a compact description of the frame. There is no separate summarizer network and no extra pass. The summary is a by-product of generating the frame.

What a frame gets to see

While frame t is being generated, each of its tokens attends to:

itself, raw tokens and summary tokens;
the last 2 frames as whole records, at full resolution;
the older frames in the window of 24, as their 96 summary tokens only;
the start image as a whole record. It is never evicted.

That is the intent: recent frames for local detail, summaries for the longer horizon, and the start image as an anchor for the scene.

One buffer, and how eviction works

All of that lives in one preallocated key/value buffer per block:
| Z0 : record(0) | RAW : 3 records, rotating | SUM : 22 x 96 summary rows, rotating |
read = buffer[0 : end]

Z0 is the start image. RAW holds the frame being generated and the 2 before it. SUM holds one 96-row summary for each older frame in the window.
When a frame falls out of the raw region, the keys and values of its 96 summary tokens are copied into SUM, over the oldest summary there, and its 1,008 raw rows are overwritten by the next frame. For example, frame 31 is written where frame 28 was, and the summary of frame 28 is written where the summary of frame 6 was.

That copy of 96 rows per block is the entire cost of moving a frame into the summary region. The order of the slots does not matter, because every key carries its own frame id in its rotary position.
Attention is then one dense read of the filled part of the buffer. There is no attention mask and nothing is concatenated: what a frame may see is decided by what is in the buffer.
With the trained window the buffer holds 6,528 keys. The same span with every frame kept whole would be 26,208.

Two smaller design details

Telling a summary from a pixel. The raw tokens and the summary tokens of a frame share the same position in time, so rotary positions alone cannot tell them apart. I did not add a token-type embedding. Each attention head has 12 temporal RoPE planes, and the two slowest ones barely rotate over the distances that occur inside the window, so they carry no usable position. Summary tokens get an exact quarter turn on those two planes. A query can then weight "summary of frame t" and "pixel of frame t" separately, using dimensions that were idle anyway.
The start image follows the window. Frame ids keep growing during a session, but the start image was written at id 0, so its distance to the live window would grow forever. RoPE keys are rotations, and rotating a stored key once more moves it forward in time. Whenever the gap between the start image and the oldest frame in memory reaches 5, the start image's keys are rotated forward, in place, to bring the gap back to 1. Values are untouched and nothing is recomputed.

One frame, start to finish

The keys you are holding become a 5-number action.
If the raw region is full, the oldest frame in it is evicted to its summary.
The new frame is denoised in three passes (t = 999, 878, 669). Each pass writes the frame's record into its slot and reads the buffer.
One more pass runs on the clean result and rewrites that slot, so the memory only ever holds clean frames.
The frame is committed and the autoencoder decodes that one latent frame into 4 RGB frames.
Those frames are encoded as H.264 and streamed to the browser.

The rest of the model

Size. 630,205,008 parameters. 28 blocks, width 1280, 20 heads of 64, SwiGLU feed-forward.
Latents. 48 channels on a /16 grid, from my own autoencoder. The start image is one latent frame, and every later latent frame is 4 RGB frames, so a window of 24 covers 96 RGB frames.
Conditioning. There is no text. I stripped the text cross-attention out for the GTA model. If you want to try the general model with text prompts, it is in this Hugging Face Space: lucidml/general-world-model. In the GTA model, the denoising timestep modulates every block, and the player's action, the frame rate and the grid shape are added to that modulation, each through its own learned gate.
Diffusion. v-prediction on a cosine noise schedule with a log-SNR shift.

Training

Everything is trained from scratch, the autoencoder too. Nothing is fine-tuned from someone else's model.
The model was pretrained on 100 million images, 4 million videos and 200,000 very long videos. It was then trained on GG800, my own dataset of about 800 hours of GTA V gameplay (100,000 videos) with recorded controls.
The release is inference only. There is no training code in the repository.

What I think is new, and what is not

I am not claiming the ingredients are new. KV caches, rotary positions and extra learned tokens all existed before this. What I have not seen put together is:

summary tokens produced by the generator's own forward pass and kept as the only trace of older frames, with whole records kept for the newest few;
one key/value buffer with a raw region and a summary region, fed by eviction and read with a single unmasked attention call;
marking the kind of a token with a fixed rotation on RoPE planes that carry no position;
rotating the cached keys of the anchor frame so it stays next to a moving window.

Limits

The memory problem is not solved. The architecture gives the model a window of 24 latent frames at a low cost, but this checkpoint was not trained to convergence, for budget reasons, so I don't know yet whether it can fully use that window. Right now it can't hold context for long.
Sessions are finite. The position table holds 4096 frame ids and a session stops at the last one. The server also has a time limit per session, 180 seconds by default.
It needs a CUDA GPU, and one GPU process serves one player at a time.

Weights

The weights and the inference code are on Hugging Face, under Apache-2.0: huggingface.co/lucidml/gta

Credits

Summaryformer is my own architecture. These are the pieces that came from other people:

Self-Forcing. The Self-Forcing repo (arXiv 2506.08009) is where I learned how a KV cache works for autoregressive video and how to run inference with one. The memory here is a different design, but that is where I learned the technique.
Wan2.1. I adapted its 3-D rotary positions, and the streaming convolutions in my autoencoder follow the Wan2.1 VAE.
Noise schedule. The cosine schedule is from Nichol and Dhariwal (arXiv 2102.09672), the log-SNR shift from Hoogeboom et al. (arXiv 2301.11093), and v-prediction from Salimans and Ho (arXiv 2202.00512).
FlashAttention and PyTorch FlexAttention for the attention kernels.
